docs:
Flags a class that declares only static members.

Dart is not Java: free-standing functions and top-level variables do not
need a class around them. A class whose every member is static — and which
therefore is never instantiated for behavior of its own — only adds a
namespace that a library (optionally imported with a prefix) already
provides. Move the members to the top level instead.

```dart
class DateUtils {           // flagged
  static DateTime mostRecent(List<DateTime> dates) => dates.last;
}

DateTime mostRecent(List<DateTime> dates) => dates.last; // preferred
```

A class holding only `static const` fields (a group of constants) is
allowed, as are sealed classes and classes with a non-default constructor.
Like the analyzer, a class is skipped when its merged interface contains an
instance member owned by a class other than `Object`; members replaced by
mixin declarations do not count. Without resolution, only local mixins are
considered member-free supertypes.
name: avoid-classes-with-only-static-members

docs:
Flags a doubly-negated boolean expression such as `!!x`.

Two `!` operators cancel out, so `!!x` is just `x`, and a longer run of
leading bangs reduces to `x` or `!x` by parity. The redundant negation adds
no meaning and obscures the value. The rule flags a `!` whose operand is
itself a `!`, reporting once at the outer negation and skipping the inner
bangs. Despite the rule's name, it targets only stacked negations — it does
not rewrite `!(a == b)` into `a != b`.
name: avoid-inverted-boolean-expressions

diagnostics.message: Unnecessary duplication of receiver.

docs:
Flags consecutive statements that invoke members on the same variable.

```dart
final list = <int>[];   // bad
list.add(1);
list.add(2);

final list = <int>[]    // good
  ..add(1)
  ..add(2);
```

Within one block (or `switch` case body) the rule follows the official
lint's cascade model. A statement that calls an instance method on, reads
a property of, sets a property of, or cascades on a simple identifier `v`
can join the preceding statement when that one targeted the same `v` and
can receive: a declaration of the local `v` (not `const`), an assignment
to the local `v` (not `??=`), a property set on a local `v` (not `??=`),
or a method call, property read, or cascade on `v`. Assignments to fields
and top-level variables never receive (the analyzer sees their setter, not
the variable), nor do property sets through them. Null-aware accesses
(`v?.m()`) and calls of static methods never join.
Method calls require a resolved non-static method: dynamic invocations and
function `call` invocations do not qualify. Parenthesized receivers are not
simple identifiers, while property assignments still accept dynamic locals.
Receiver types come from shared resolution, including imported top-level
getters/variables and implicit method calls used as cascade initializers;
genuinely unresolved receivers stay silent rather than guessing a method.

A statement whose member names, arguments, or right-hand side depend on
the receiver breaks the chain, since a cascade would evaluate them before
the earlier member access: a reference to the same local declaration (not
a shadowing closure parameter), and for a field or top-level-variable receiver
also a closure or a reference to any member declared in the same class as
the field (respectively any top-level declaration of the same library).
One diagnostic covers each run of
joinable statements, from the first statement that could be cascaded to
the last one. Where falcon cannot resolve a referenced member's declaring
class (for example through an external type), it assumes a dependency and
stays silent.
name: cascade-invocations

docs:
Flags a function whose cyclomatic complexity exceeds the configured threshold.

Cyclomatic complexity counts the independent paths through a function; a high
value means many branches to understand and test. The rule computes
complexity as one plus each decision point — `if`, ternary, `&&`, `||`, `??`,
loops (`for`/`while`/`do`), `catch` clauses, non-default `case`s, and pattern
`when` guards — counted across the whole body tree, so decision points inside
nested closures and local functions count toward the enclosing function. It
reports at the function name when the total exceeds the threshold.
Operator bodies are included. Collection `if`/`for` elements are not decision
points themselves, but decisions in their conditions and children are counted.
Parameter defaults are constant expressions, not runtime body decisions, and
are excluded for both the declaration and its nested functions.

## Options

`max_complexity` (integer, default: 20) — flag when the computed complexity
exceeds this.
name: cyclomatic-complexity

docs:
Flags an assignment immediately followed by `return` of the same variable.

When a block ends with `x = e; return x;` the two statements can be joined
into `return x = e;` (or simply `return e;` for a local). The rule looks at
the last two statements of every block: the second-to-last must be an
assignment (any operator), increment, decrement, or other prefix/postfix
expression on the same variable or property chain that the final `return`
yields. A run of assignments to that same target (`x = a; x += b; return
x;`) is left alone, as are switch-case statement lists, which are not blocks.

```dart
int f(int a) {
  a += 1; // flagged
  return a;
}
```

Flags a function whose control-flow nesting runs deeper than the configured level.

Deeply nested blocks push logic to the right and make control flow hard to
follow; early returns, guard clauses, and extracted helpers flatten it. The

included; the rule reports at the declaration when depth exceeds the threshold.

docs:
Prefers collection `if` elements to conditional expressions in list and set literals.

Since Dart 2.3 a list or set literal can choose an element with an `if`
element, so `[a, b ? c : d]` reads better as `[a, if (b) c else d]`. The rule
flags a conditional expression that is itself a list or set element, or the
`then`/`else` element of a collection `if`, or the body of a collection `for`.
Conditionals nested deeper inside an element (`[f(b ? c : d)]`) and map
entries are left alone, as the official lint does.
name: prefer-if-elements-to-conditional-expressions

Flags `x == null ? y : x` (and the inverted `x != null ? x : y`).

docs:
Flags a closure that only forwards its parameters to a function a tear-off could name.

`names.forEach((name) { print(name); })` allocates a closure whose whole job
is to call `print`; `names.forEach(print)` says the same thing. The rule
fires on an anonymous, synchronous closure whose body is a single
invocation — `=> f(a, b)`, `{ f(a, b); }`, or `{ return f(a, b); }` —
passing exactly the closure's positional parameters in order and named
parameters under the same names, and on `(a) => C(a)` constructor calls a
`C.new` tear-off could replace. Like the analyzer, this does not compare
optional parameter defaults. The invoked function must stay the same object
between calls:

- a top-level, local, static, or instance method, or a `final`, non-`late`
  variable or field holding a function (the analyzer does not count a
  `const` variable, field, or enum value as final);
- reached through a receiver that is a class name, an import prefix, or a
  `final` variable or field (including immutable record fields), never
  through `this`, a parameter of the closure, or a null-aware access (`a?.b`).
  A member falcon cannot resolve
  on a stable receiver is taken to be a method, as the analyzer treats any
  member that is not a getter.

A function or method is itself a stable receiver, including `p.call(x)`.
Optional constructor parameters do not prevent a tear-off from replacing
a required-parameter closure when the constructor accepts those arguments.
An optional closure parameter must stay optional on the target; legacy
`@required` annotations do not change that shape. Constructor invocations
with named arguments are excluded, matching the analyzer.
Optional positional super formals retain their optional shape even when
their inherited default value is unavailable.

Generic method invocations with explicit type arguments, calls through
deferred imports, and `const` constructor calls are skipped. A constructor
call only counts in an arrow body, and the constructor tear-off must fit the
closure's type, so every closure parameter's type must be known (written or
supplied by the context). When the closure is a named argument or a variable
initializer, a method tear-off must also fit the closure's type: the
parameter types must be known, and a block body that discards the call must
be in a `void`-returning context (otherwise the closure returns `Null`).

falcon stays silent when it cannot resolve the invoked function or receiver.
Constructor calls are only checked when constructor tear-offs are enabled
(language version 2.15 or later); before that, `(a) => C(a)` is silent.
name: unnecessary-lambdas

Receiver and callback must match: removing a different callback or listening

description: Disallow relative imports in libraries under a package's `lib/` directory.
docs:
Disallow relative imports in libraries under a package's `lib/` directory.

The rule runs
only for files inside the enclosing package's `lib/` directory (the nearest
`pubspec.yaml` decides the package; files outside any package are skipped,
like the analyzer's `isInLibDir`). Every `import` whose URI parses with an
empty scheme is reported, so `import 'src/a.dart';` must be spelled
`import 'package:<name>/src/a.dart';`. `package:` and `dart:` imports,
exports, and conditional alternatives are not checked; relative imports that
reach into `lib/` from outside it belong to `avoid_relative_lib_imports`.
Incompatible with `prefer-relative-imports`.
name: always-use-package-imports

docs:
Avoid method calls or property accesses on a `dynamic` target.

Members reached through `dynamic` are looked up at runtime: typos and
signature mismatches surface as `NoSuchMethodError` instead of compile
errors, and the dispatch is slower:

```dart
void log(dynamic event) {
  print(event.name); // BAD
}

void log(Event event) {
  print(event.name); // GOOD
}
```

Reported targets: member accesses, method calls, index operations,
user-definable binary operators (not `==`/`!=`), prefix and postfix
operators, and compound assignments on a `dynamic` receiver, plus calls of a
`dynamic` or `Function`-typed variable, including `.call()` cascade sections.
`hashCode`, `runtimeType`, `toString`, and `noSuchMethod` — members every
object has — are allowed (except method calls directly on cascade targets),
as are explicit `as dynamic` casts and `x!`.

Receiver and callable types come from the semantic resolver, including
flow-promoted types at each use site.
Diagnostics retain grouped receiver spans; compound updates use the complete
update expression, and selector chains retain their cascade-section start.
name: avoid-dynamic-calls

declared `const` or plain `final`, including `late final`, which can still be
assigned once at an arbitrary point. Mutable global state is reachable and
writable from anywhere, which makes data flow hard to trace, introduces
initialization-order and concurrency hazards, and lets tests contaminate one

docs:
Avoid `Type.toString()` in production code, where type names may be minified.

Web and AOT builds may minify or strip type names, so a string built from a
`Type` can differ between debug and release:

```dart
class TypeName implements Type {}
final name = TypeName().toString(); // BAD: uses `Object.toString`
if (value is Widget) {} // GOOD: compare types, not their names
```

A `toString` invocation (cascade sections included) or a `toString`
tear-off passed as an argument is reported when it resolves to
`Object.toString` and its target type is a non-nullable subtype of
`dart:core` `Type`. The target type is the receiver's static type when that
is an interface type; otherwise (no receiver, `dynamic`, a type parameter)
it is the type of the most recent class, mixin, or extension declaration
in the file — the official visitor never resets it, so it carries over into
later functions, enums, and extension types. A tear-off through a simple
identifier prefix (`t.toString`) uses only an interface-typed prefix.
`Type` itself (and so every `runtimeType` read) is never reported, because
`dart:core` `Type` redeclares `toString`.
name: avoid-type-to-string

docs:
Flags local futures first awaited after another await inside a try/catch.

A future can complete with an unhandled error while execution is suspended,
before the later await attaches the surrounding catch's error handler. Await
it immediately or attach an error handler before the first async gap.

This conservative analysis follows straight-line statements directly in a
try body with at least one catch. It tracks resolved Future-returning calls
and constructors assigned to locals, and reports the later awaited local,
not discarded futures. Unknown base types and FutureOr are excluded. Early
catchError, onError, and then(onError:) calls are exempt, including handlers
attached in a separate statement or initializer. Parentheses are transparent.
Branches, loops, nested blocks, local declarations of functions, and other
expression statements end tracking: no control-flow or alias assumptions are
made across them. Late and multi-variable declarations are excluded. Nested
functions and shadowed locals cannot consume an outer candidate. Only root
await expressions in expression, return, and local-variable statements count
as gaps; awaits nested in other expressions are outside the matching limits.
A reference inside a composite await operand conservatively consumes that
candidate, covering combinators and forwarding methods without alias guesses.
A handler protects only the call it terminates, not subsequent chained calls.
When intermediate types are unavailable, only SDK Future method chains
(then/catchError/onError/timeout/whenComplete) on a proven Future base qualify.
name: avoid-uncaught-future-errors

A subscription that is never cancelled keeps its stream (and everything the
listener captures) alive, leaking memory and running callbacks after their
owner is gone:

```dart
class Watcher {
  StreamSubscription<int>? _sub; // BAD: never cancelled
}

class Watcher {
  StreamSubscription<int>? _sub;
  void dispose() => _sub?.cancel(); // GOOD
}
```

`StreamSubscription` are reported unless the file (fields) or enclosing
function body (locals) holds an official valid-use/escape case. Constructor
arguments and assignments into another local do not escape; references to
shadowing variables never cancel the original. Unresolved types stay silent.

directive messages use canonical package URIs, and local functions stay within
their lexical block, switch case, or unbraced statement body. Deprecation messages
are trimmed and punctuated like the analyzer's messages. Membership is cached per source.
Cascade diagnostics consume shared semantic traversal callbacks, including
receiver inference and indexed-assignment classification.
Extension owners honor inferred arguments and bounds; `super` owners follow
concrete mixin constraints before interface contracts. Optional parameter
deprecations are checked even when the enclosing member is not deprecated.
Explicit construction resolves dotted constructor selectors separately from
import prefixes; generic class qualifiers retain their constructor metadata.
Constructor aliases resolve to the underlying declaration before constructor
and deprecated-parameter metadata is inspected. Compound assignments and
increments inspect both accessors, while simple assignments inspect only setters.
Local metadata follows binding declaration identities, including loop variables;
local function metadata also applies to references before its lexical declaration.
Enum constants do not name deprecated constructors; implicit extension operators
use the same applicable-extension lookup as ordinary members.
Member and parameter selectors borrow names and keep declaration kind, access,
and static dispatch distinct; retained metadata owns names only during indexing.
Grouped references are visited, but grouped callees do not expose declaration
parameter metadata as direct invocations do.
Null-shortened receiver chains recover reached declaration types until parentheses,
preserving declared nullable members and applicable nullable extensions.
Named constructor uses cover their full qualifier; implicit super uses cover
the complete constructor declaration that makes the implicit call.
name: deprecated-member-use-from-same-package

docs:
Don't discard `Future`s returned by calls in synchronous functions.

A `Future` created inside a non-`async` function and then dropped can't be
awaited, so its errors and completion are lost:

```dart
void save() {
  writeFile(); // BAD
}

Future<void> save() async {
  await writeFile(); // GOOD
}
```

Expression statements, cascade sections, and string interpolations whose
resolved type is `Future` (or a subtype) or `FutureOr` are reported inside
synchronous bodies. Assignments, `Future.delayed(duration, computation)`,
`Map.putIfAbsent`, and members annotated `@awaitNotRequired`, including
inherited, extension, and local functions, are exempt; local annotations
follow the visible declaration rather than a reusable name. Function typedef
annotations follow the invoked value's immediate alias through inferred
variables, fields, records, and collections, but not explicit `.call` or an
unannotated alias of that typedef. Member calls, including null-aware
accesses, use the reached receiver branch for annotation lookup, as do
bounded type parameters and flow-promoted `FutureOr` values. Unresolved
types stay silent. Calls through getters underline the complete callee expression,
while method invocations underline only the method name.
name: discarded-futures

docs:
Flags classes that implicitly reopen a supertype declared in the same
library.

Class modifiers are only enforced across library boundaries, so inside its
own library an `interface` or `final` class can be extended by a class that
drops the restriction — silently letting other libraries extend what the
author meant to close. Mark the subclass with the same modifier, or annotate
it with package:meta's `@reopen` when reopening is intended.

```dart
interface class I {}
class C extends I {}          // flagged: reopens 'I' (not marked 'interface')

final class F {}
base class B extends F {}     // flagged: reopens 'F' (not marked 'final')
```

Sealed and `mixin` classes and classes annotated with `@reopen` are exempt.
Only superclasses declared in the same library (this file or its parts) are
considered, including named mixin applications. A sealed superclass carries
the modifier its own supertypes induce (a sealed subclass of an `interface`
class is an interface).

ANALYZER-BUG: the analyzer can miss reopening when a sealed class is declared
before its sealed superclass. Falcon computes the induced restriction
independently of that declaration order.
name: implicit-reopen

description: Reports inline test callbacks that contain no recognized assertion calls.
docs:
Reports inline test callbacks that contain no recognized assertion calls.

Only `_test.dart` files importing `test` or `flutter_test` are inspected,
and `test`/`testWidgets` must resolve to a framework package. Assertions
include framework expectations, asynchronous expectation wrappers, `fail`,
and mockito/mocktail verification calls. Assertions in unused local closures
or functions and nested tests do not satisfy the enclosing test.

## Options

`include-assertions` is a list of additional assertion function names. These
names explicitly trust project helpers, including local functions; prefixed
names can be supplied as written at their call sites.

import 'package:test/test.dart';

As in the analyzer's expected-type helper, only these positions have an
expected type:

- a returned or yielded value (also awaited) of a function declaration
  with a declared return type (an `async` function's `Future` argument),
  or of a closure or untyped local function whose block body's returns
  infer `T` or `T?`; methods have none;
- a variable's initializer: its declared type, and for an untyped local or

- the value (also awaited) of a plain `=` assignment, except `x = x!` and
  `a.b = a.b!`;

  constructor-initializer `super(...)`/`this(...)` arguments; an awaited
  right operand or positional argument has none;
- an element of a list or set literal, a key or value of a map literal
  (through the map's collection `if` and `for` elements); an awaited or
  parenthesized map key expects the map's value type.

patterns have none. Inferred types never keep the `T & Object`
intersection of `x!`. Flow analysis promotes a local after its `x!`.

Flags uses of the `Null` type where `void` is meant.

`Null` and `void` both describe "no useful value", but `void` says the value
must not be used while `Null` admits only `null` and is a subtype of every
nullable type. Writing `Future<Null>` or a `Null` return type usually means
`void`, and only `void` lets implementations return whatever they like.

```dart
Null f() {}                   // flagged
Future<Null> g() async {}     // flagged
void h() {}                   // preferred
```

Following the official lint, `Null` is accepted where `void` cannot replace
it: casts (`as Null`, cast patterns), local and top-level variable types,
the return and parameter types written directly in a function type, type
arguments of empty collection literals (`<Null>[]`), `extension on Null`,
extension type representations, and return types of members overriding a
member that does not return `void` after substituting inherited type arguments.
Overrides whose external declarations are unavailable are conservatively
exempt; an unresolved source superclass is not evidence of an override.
name: prefer-void-to-null

method when no call site anywhere in the project passes it null, and its body

docs:
Flags expression statements whose expression has no clear effect.

A statement such as `x;`, `1 + 2;`, `list.clear;` or `c ? a : b;` computes a
value and throws it away, which usually means the author forgot a call, an
assignment, or a `return`. Expressions with a clear effect are allowed:
assignments, invocations, instance creations, `await`, `throw`, `rethrow`,
cascades, `as` casts, postfix operators (`x++`, `x!`) and prefix `++`/`--`.
The right operand of `&&`, `||`, and `??`, and both branches of a
conditional, are checked in turn, since those operators are used for control
flow. A parenthesized expression is always reported, as are binary
operations, index reads, literals, and `is` tests.

Identifiers and resolved property reads are reported unless they denote an
explicitly declared getter, which may have side effects. Dynamic reads and
unresolved identifiers are reported too. Applicable extension getters are
allowed, while property reads of unavailable external members are
conservatively left alone. The same checks apply to the initializer and
updaters of a `for (;;)` loop with an expression initializer. A cascade
section that reads a method or function-valued member (`..clear`) is reported.
Constructor and generic function tear-offs are references without an effect.
Reading a function's synthetic `call` member is also a tear-off, including
null-aware reads and cascade sections; invoking it still has an effect.

```dart
void f(List<int> list, int a, int b) {
  a;          // flagged
  list.clear; // flagged
  a + b;      // flagged
  list.clear(); // ok
}
```
name: unnecessary-statements

Flags a public top-level declaration in `lib/` — a class, mixin, enum,

(`_`-prefixed) declarations are out of scope. This is a cross-file rule: it
runs in the cross-file pass over the whole analyzed file set and is
configured under the top-level `cross-file` section rather than `linter`.

diagnostics.message: File is not reachable from any entrypoint (main, a non-lib file, or the public library surface); it may be dead code

docs:
Report `lib/` files that no project entrypoint can reach.

Models the file set as a directed graph (file → every file its
imports/exports/parts reference) and flags a `lib/src/**` file when no
entrypoint reaches it. Entrypoints ("roots") are: any analyzed file outside
`lib/` (bin/test/tool/example, or their own concern), any file declaring a
top-level `main`, and the public library surface — every `lib/` file not
under `lib/src/`, which external packages may import (this subsumes the
`lib/<pkg>.dart` barrel). Reachability, not mere reference count, is the test:
a cluster of `lib/src` files that reference only each other but that nothing
live reaches is dead and is flagged. `part of` files belong to their owning
library and are never flagged directly. Without a pubspec the scope narrows
to files with a `lib/` path component and the public-surface exemption is not
applied (no `lib/` root is known). This is a cross-file rule: it runs in the
cross-file pass and is configured under the top-level `cross-file` section.
name: unused-files

```dart

```

Arguments of direct function, method, and constructor invocations, assignments
(including assigned-variable patterns and cascades), and index assignments
are checked against the instantiated parameter type, including receiver and
inferred method type arguments in cascade calls: a `void` location accepts only
`void`, `Null`, `Never`, and `Future`s of those; a `FutureOr<void>` location
additionally accepts `dynamic` and any `FutureOr` or `Future` of an
acceptable type. Only block-bodied function literals have their inferred
return type checked, inferring the literal against the location's type;
expression bodies and tear-offs are not checked as callbacks. Return
statements use the enclosing function's return type (a function literal's
inferred one, not its context); returning to `void` is checked only for a
`dynamic` value. Assignments and returns report at the whole statement,
arguments at the value expression.

an explicit `.call(...)` remains a method invocation and is checked.

grouping a direct invocation does not exclude the invocation itself.

docs:
Flags `==` and `hashCode` overrides in classes not marked `@immutable`.

A value-based `==` and `hashCode` on a mutable object is a trap: once the
object is stored in a `Set` or used as a `Map` key, mutating it changes its
hash code and the collection silently loses track of it. Only classes that
are (transitively) annotated with package:meta's `@immutable` should
override them.

```dart

  int x;
  Point(this.x);
  @override
  bool operator ==(Object other) => other is Point && other.x == x; // flagged
  @override
  int get hashCode => x.hashCode; // flagged
}
```

mixin, or interface). Unresolved supertypes leave immutability unknown.

docs:
Flags arguments that pass exactly the parameter's default value.

An optional parameter's default already applies when the argument is
omitted, so `f(flag: false)` against `void f({bool flag = false})` is noise.
The rule compares each constant argument with the constant default of the
optional parameter it binds to and reports matches. Arguments are visited
from last to first, stopping after the first optional positional parameter:
an earlier positional argument may be needed to reach a later one. For a
redirecting factory constructor the defaults of the final redirect target
apply. Required parameters and `@required` ones are never reported.

Defaults come from indexed callable declarations, local functions and
function-valued locals, and the `call` method of callable objects. An optional
parameter without a declared default defaults to `null`; a super formal
inherits its super parameter's default.
Members of generic declarations whose function type mentions the owner's
type parameters are skipped: the analyzer invokes them through a
substituted type whose parameters carry no defaults. Values are evaluated
in the default's declaring library (including external named extensions)
and captured local constant scope, and the caller's lexical context separately.
Values that cannot be folded are skipped; the analyzer's unknown web
environment booleans remain unknown even with an explicit fallback.

docs:
Requires overriding methods to keep the positional parameter names of the
member they inherit.

The rule only runs for libraries under the package's `lib/` directory and skips
static and documented methods. For a class, enum, or mixin class the
compared member is the concrete one inherited through the superclass chain
and mixin applications (abstract and `implements`-only members do not
count); for a mixin it is the member of its `on` types' interfaces (or
`Object`). Owners with private names, extension types, getters, and setters
are never checked. Positional parameters are compared pairwise up to the
shorter list.

A `_` name on either side is skipped when the library's language version
enables wildcard variables (3.7+).

docs:
Flags type annotations on closure parameters whose types come from context.

When a function expression is passed where a function type is expected,
its parameter types are inferred from that type, so annotating them is
redundant. Closures without a known function-typed context are left alone
because their annotations carry information. Like the official lint, a
closure that is an operand, an `await` operand, a switch expression arm,
a record literal field, or a direct collection literal element/key/value
(including collection `if`/`for`) has no context here. This does not suppress
independently contextualized callbacks nested inside those expressions.
Parenthesizing an operand (including the fallback of `??`) does not add context.
A returned closure has context only in an `async` body returning `Future<F>`
for a function type `F`. A conditional branch or assignment RHS takes its
enclosing expression's own static type as its context, including function
types obtained by joining variant signatures. Joins retain the shared
optional positional prefix when required arity agrees. Different required
arities join to general `Function`, unless a concrete downward function
context provides a shared signature.

```dart
names.map((String name) => name.length); // flagged
names.map((name) => name.length);        // ok
```
name: avoid-types-on-closure-parameters

A constructor parameter that is neither read by an initializer nor by the
body is dead weight that every caller still has to supply. Initializing
formals (`this.x`) and super parameters (`super.x`) are always used, and
parameters annotated `@deprecated`/`@Deprecated(...)` or named only with
underscores are skipped, as are redirecting factory and `external`
constructors. Primary header parameters are also read by eager instance
field initializers; declaring primary parameters implicitly initialize fields.

```dart
}
```

docs:
Avoid `async` functions and methods declared to return `void`.

Callers cannot await a `void` result, so they cannot know when the work has
finished or observe its errors. Return `Future<void>` instead:

```dart
void save() async {} // BAD
Future<void> save() async {} // GOOD
```

written return type are skipped: an override may inherit `void`, which only
full type resolution can see.

Writing the constant first — `if (0 == count)` — is the "Yoda condition"

how the comparison is spoken and scanned. The check covers the equality and
relational operators (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=`) whenever the left

against another literal (as in `null == null`) is left alone.

expressions, initializers, and collections.

docs:
Flags boolean identifiers that lack a conventional interrogative prefix.

A boolean named `visible` reads as a value, whereas `isVisible` reads as the
yes/no question it answers; a consistent prefix (`is`, `has`, `can`, ...)
makes conditions self-documenting. Only variables and fields initialized
with a boolean *literal*, and `bool`-returning methods, getters, and
functions, are checked — parameters and uninitialized fields are not. A
single leading underscore is stripped before matching, and `@override`
members are exempt because they cannot rename an inherited declaration.

## Options

`valid_prefixes` (list of strings, default: `["is", "are", "was", "were",
"has", "have", "had", "can", "should", "will", "do", "does", "did"]`) —
accepted boolean-name prefixes. User-provided entries extend the defaults
rather than replacing them.
name: boolean-prefixes

docs:
Flags class members declared out of a canonical order.

A consistent member layout lets readers find fields, constructors, and
methods in the same place across every class. Without options the built-in
order applies: static constants, static fields, instance `final` fields,
instance mutable fields, constructors, public getters and setters, public
methods, then private members. Members are ranked by category and any pair
found out of sequence is reported.

## Options

`order` (list of category tokens, default: the built-in order above) — the
required member sequence. Supported tokens are `public-fields`,
`private-fields`, `fields`, `static-fields`, `constructors`,
`named-constructors`, `static-methods`, `private-methods`, `public-methods`,
`methods`, `getters`, and `setters`. A member is ranked by the earliest
token it qualifies for; members matching no token are ignored.
name: class-members-ordering

docs:
Require the targets of conditional import and export URIs to exist.

Every
configurable URI (`if (dart.library.io) 'io_impl.dart'`) on an `import` or
`export` is resolved as the analyzer resolves it, and reported when it
names no existing source:

- A relative URI resolves against the URI of the containing file: its
  `package:` URI inside a package's `lib/` directory, so climbing out of
  `lib/` names another package, else its `file:` URI.
- A `package:` URI resolves through the package configuration. Without one,
  every `package:` URI is reported. A query is ignored; a fragment, an
  unknown package, or a missing path segment is reported.
- A `file:` URI needs an absolute path; its authority is ignored. A query or
  fragment (including on a relative URI resolved to `file:`) names no file.
- A `dart:` URI must name a library of the SDK (with its embedder); without
  a located SDK only invalid paths, queries and fragments are reported.
- Any other scheme is reported.

Invalid schemes and invalid percent escapes still name missing sources;
invalid percent escapes are interpreted as literal percent signs.
The default (unconditional) URI is not checked by this rule.
Package and SDK metadata come from the run's shared analysis environment;
callers must attach it to resolve configured package sources.
name: conditional-uri-does-not-exist

docs:
Requires curly braces around the bodies of flow-control statements.

A brace-less body invites the "goto fail" class of bug, where a later edit
adds a second statement that silently falls outside the branch. Requiring
blocks around `for`, `while`, `do`, and `if`/`else` bodies keeps the scope
explicit and edits safe. Two carve-outs match the official lint: an `if`
with no `else` whose body sits on the same line as its condition may omit
braces, and an `else if` chain need not wrap the intermediate `if` in a
block.

docs:
Flags import and export directives that break the Effective Dart ordering.

Directives are grouped into sections — `dart:` first, then `package:`, then
relative URIs — with exports in their own section after every import, and each
section sorted alphabetically. Every directive is reported at most once, with
the first broken convention in this order:

```dart
import 'package:a/a.dart';
import 'dart:async';          // flagged: 'dart:' imports go first
import 'package:c/c.dart';
import 'package:b/b.dart';    // flagged: sort sections alphabetically
import 'x.dart';
export 'y.dart';              // flagged: exports go after all imports
import 'package:d/d.dart';    // flagged: 'package:' before relative
```

All `package:` directives form one section; the analyzer does not separate
the current package from third-party packages. `@docImport`s of the library
documentation comment form their own sections, checked like imports.
name: directives-ordering

docs:
Flags comments that are not formatted as complete sentences.

Sentence-cased, terminated comments read consistently and signal a finished
thought rather than a scratch note. A comment should start with an uppercase
letter and end with `.`, `!`, `?`, or `:`. Consecutive comment lines are
joined into one block and split into sentences before checking, so a sentence
that wraps across several `///` lines is judged as a whole and continuation
lines are never flagged on their own. Both `//` line comments and `///` doc
comments are checked by default.

## Options

`only_doc_comments` (bool, default: `false`) — when `true`, only `///` doc
comments are checked.

`ignored_patterns` (list of regexes, default: `[]`) — a comment matching any
of these patterns is skipped entirely; invalid patterns are ignored.
name: format-comment

docs:
Flags class members declared out of the configured order.

A predictable member layout makes classes easier to navigate. Without
options the built-in order applies: static constants, static fields, instance
fields, constructors, static methods, then instance methods. Members are
ranked by category and any pair out of sequence is reported. For Flutter
`State` subclasses, a separate lifecycle ordering can be enforced with
`widgets_order`.

## Options

`order` (list of category tokens, default: the built-in order above) — the
required member sequence. Supported tokens are `public-fields`,
`private-fields`, `fields`, `static-fields`, `constructors`,
`named-constructors`, `static-methods`, `private-methods`, `public-methods`,
`methods`, `getters`, and `setters`. A member is ranked by the earliest
token it qualifies for; members matching no token are ignored.

`widgets_order` (list of lifecycle tokens, default: none) — for a class that
`extends State`, orders lifecycle members by this list. Supported tokens:
`constructor`, `init-state`, `did-change-dependencies`, `did-update-widget`,
`dispose`, `build`, and `overridden-methods`.
name: member-ordering

abstract classes are exempt. Extension-target checks are syntactic: an
unqualified named target is checked only if it names a non-abstract class
declared in this file, `Object`, or one of the extension's type parameters.

prefixed targets, external classes and `Never`; this is not a semantic test

supplies iteration semantics but is not the iterable's own static type.

method calls, and inferred `for-in` bindings participate without SDK sources.

Don't reassign parameters of functions, methods, or constructors.

Rebinding a parameter makes the body harder to follow: the name no longer
means what the caller passed. Assignments (`x = ...`, `x += ...`),
increments and decrements, and pattern assignments (`(x, y) = ...`) that
write a parameter are flagged, including writes from closures inside the
body. One exception mirrors the analyzer: an optional parameter without a
default value (so it defaults to `null`) may be given a default once with
`x ??= value`; a second `??=` or any other assignment is still flagged.
The analyzer also exempts increments/decrements of optional parameters
without defaults, and this rule retains that exception.

Like the analyzer's visitor, the search does not descend into an assignment
expression unless that assignment itself writes the parameter and the
parameter defaults to `null`: writes nested in any other assignment
(`target[offset++] = v`, `x = p++`, `c.onCancel = () { p = 0; }`,
`a..v = (p = 2)`) are not reported. A constructor's parameters are searched
for in its body only, not in its initializer list.

```dart

void g([int? x]) { x ??= 2; } // ok
```

docs:
Flags no-argument collection constructor calls that a literal would express.

The empty `List()`, `Map()`, `Set()`, `LinkedHashMap()`, and `LinkedHashSet()`
constructors are more verbose than the equivalent `[]` or `{}` literals, which
are the idiomatic way to build a fresh collection and read more clearly. The
rule matches the unnamed and `.new` constructors written as a plain call
(`List()`, `Set.new()`), an explicit `new` expression (`new Map()`), or with
type arguments (`Map<K, V>()`). It deliberately spares named constructors such
as `List.filled` or `Map.of` and any invocation carrying arguments, since
those have no literal form.

Two further facts withhold a diagnostic that would otherwise change semantics:

* **Concrete context** — a `LinkedHashMap()` / `LinkedHashSet()` whose declared
  context type (a variable/field/top-level/return annotation) *is* that concrete
  type. A `{}` literal has static type `Map`/`Set`, which is not assignable back
  to `LinkedHashMap`/`LinkedHashSet`, so the constructor is required. This check
  is purely syntactic and applies without a type index. Local functions and
  operators use their own return annotations, never their enclosing function's.
* **Shadowed or unresolved identity** — a `List()`/`Map()`/`Set()`/… whose
  resolved declaration is not the SDK collection, or whose library/import
  graph cannot establish that identity. A literal could construct a different
  type. Without an identity index, the rule remains syntactic and such a
  constructor keeps firing.

Everything else — including any `var`/unannotated context, and a concrete
constructor reached only through a nested argument position — keeps firing.
name: prefer-collection-literals

Prefers `const` when invoking a `const` constructor with constant arguments.

When a constructor is declared `const` and the invocation would be a valid
constant expression (constant arguments the constructor accepts, set
elements and map keys with primitive equality, no type parameters in type
arguments), invoking it with `const` produces a canonicalized instance
instead of allocating a new one. The rule flags such invocations outside a
constant context (where `const` is already implied). It stays silent when
the constructor cannot be resolved to a declaration known to be `const`,
when an argument cannot be proven constant, for `Object()` (often used to create
unique identity tokens), for constructors of deferred-imported classes, and
for a generic class invoked without type arguments whose approximate context
contains type parameters. As in the analyzer, assignments use their result
type rather than their target type.

```dart
class A {
  const A();
}

final a = A();       // BAD
final b = const A(); // GOOD
```

docs:
Suggests collapsing compatible nested layout widgets into one `Container`.

Matches at least three Flutter widgets in Container's outside-in order:
`Transform`, margin `Padding`, `ConstrainedBox`, `ColoredBox`, inner `Padding`,
and `Align`. Stages may be omitted, but not repeated or reordered. Only the
unnamed constructors and their directly equivalent arguments qualify; inner
keys, alignment size factors, transform origins and hit-test overrides are
excluded. Decoration and clipping are excluded because their padding and
clipping behavior cannot generally be reproduced by a Container. The final
child must be provably non-null to preserve Container's empty-child behavior.
Constant contexts are excluded because Container has no const constructor.
A concrete source-widget expected type is also excluded to preserve typing.

## Options

`min_sequence` (integer, default: 3) sets the minimum chain length, with a
minimum effective value of 3 to avoid competing with single-widget rules.

Flags declared identifiers that are shorter or longer than the allowed range.

Very short names rarely convey meaning and very long ones hurt readability, so
this rule keeps declared names within a configurable length band. Its scope is
deliberately limited to variable and field declarations, getter and setter
names, and enum constants; parameters, catch-clause variables, for-each loop
variables, and plain function and method names are never checked, because
short names are often idiomatic there. A single leading underscore is stripped
before both the length and exception checks, so `_id` is judged as `id`.
Declarations in initializer closures, arrow bodies, operators, and enum
members follow the same policy as declarations in ordinary function bodies.

## Options

`min_length` (int, default: 3) — flag identifiers shorter than this.
`max_length` (int, default: 300) — flag identifiers longer than this.
`exceptions` (list of strings, default: []) — names always allowed regardless of length.

docs:
Flags a private field that is initialized but never reassigned, so it could
be `final` (`prefer-final-fields`, adopted from package:lints).

Marking such fields `final` documents that they never change after
construction and lets the compiler enforce it, preventing accidental
mutation. The analysis is deliberately conservative to avoid false positives:
a whole-*library* scan first records every name that is ever assigned,
compound assigned, or incremented, and any such write disqualifies that name
(matched by identifier across the library, so a like-named field in another
class also protects it). A candidate is reported only when it is provably
initialized through the channels recognized by the analyzer: every declared
constructor setting it via `: _x = ...` or a `this._x` formal, or a declaration
initializer when no constructor sets it. Enum fields are exempt. Only
private (underscore-prefixed) fields are considered, and those already
`final`, `const`, `late`, `external`, or `abstract` are skipped.

Library awareness (suppress-only): a private field can be written from a
sibling part file, so write collection unions this file with every sibling in
its [`AnalyzeContext::library`]. When the library has an unresolved part, or
this file declares `part`/`part of` directives but no library context is
available, the full set of writes cannot be seen — every private-field
diagnostic for the file is suppressed rather than risk a false positive. A
standalone file with no part directives keeps the exact single-file behavior.
name: prefer-final-fields

Prefer `final` for a for-each loop variable that is never reassigned.

`for (var item in items)` where `item` is never written in its scope reads
better as `for (final item in items)`. Destructuring loops are covered when
the top-level record, object, list, or map pattern binds only plain
variables and none of them is reassigned. A loop over an existing variable
(`for (item in items)`) declares nothing and is ignored. Collection loops
outside function bodies (top-level and field initializers) are also ignored.

top-level variable and field initializers) are not reported.

docs:
Documents public declarations and members in package libraries.

Private declarations, top-level functions named `main`, and overriding members are
exempt; like the analyzer, `package:meta`'s `@internal` exempts a top-level
declaration with its members, but not a member on its own. Ordinary constructors
of enums and of sealed, `abstract final` and `abstract interface` classes are exempt.
A doc comment
before, between or after the metadata documents the declaration, including
the analyzer's empty `/**/` documentation. `@override` alone does not exempt
a member. Fields and getters override inherited getters, methods and fields
(not setters);
setters override inherited setters and are checked only when their paired
getter is reported. Extension-type
representation fields are not field declarations visited by the upstream
rule.
A class primary constructor is checked separately from its type; header
constructors are reported at their name without closed-type exemptions,
and implementations at `this`. Header parameters are not field declarations.

same-named declaration among incompatible inherited interface signatures.

examples.good:

Flags a multi-line call, declaration, assert, or collection literal that is
missing a trailing comma.

When the opening and closing delimiters of an argument list, parameter list,
`assert`, or list/set/map literal sit on different lines, the last element
must be followed by a comma so the formatter keeps one element per line:

```dart
foo(a, b);                    // fine: fits on one line
foo(
  a,
  b                           // flagged at `)`
);
void f({
  required int a              // flagged at `}`
}) {}
```

A positional last element that itself spans several lines is exempt when it
is a block-bodied function literal, a string literal, an immediately
invoked function literal whose arguments fit on one line, or a list, set, or
map literal — the classic `test('name', () { ... });` shape. Named
arguments and parameters never get the exemption. Record literals, type
argument lists, and extension type representation clauses are not checked.

Delimiters inside string interpolations (`'${f(a, b)}'`) are matched like
any others.

Like the official lint, the rule is off in libraries at language version
3.7 or later, where the formatter's tall style owns trailing commas.

not null, the parameter should declare a non-nullable type instead, so the
check happens at compile time. The assert must be `assert(x != null)` or

type for an untyped `super.x`. A trailing `?` or `dynamic` proves

unresolved types are never reported. The analyzer treats an undefined type

undefined type from one declared in a library it does not load.

identifier/null test. Repeated asserts on one formal produce one diagnostic.

A public API's types are part of its contract; leaving them to inference
(or `dynamic`) makes the contract implicit and easy to break. Public
top-level functions and methods need a return type (setters and
`operator []=` excepted), their parameters need types, and public fields
and top-level variables need a declared type unless they are `const`, or

checked too.

fields and top-level variables, flagging closure parameters and locals
declared there; falcon checks only the declarations themselves, since those

docs:
Flags a *redundant* type annotation on an initializing formal or super
parameter (`type-init-formals`, adopted from package:lints).

In `C(int this.x)` or `C(int super.x)` the annotation restates a type the
field (or super-parameter) already fixes, so it adds nothing and risks
drifting out of sync with that declaration. It is redundant only when it
names the *same* type: annotating a narrower one — `num x; C(int this.x);` —
is legal Dart that meaningfully restricts the constructor's parameter, and
upstream (`nodeType.type == field.type`) does not report it.

Falcon limitation: this rule compares written types after whitespace
normalization, not semantic type equality. Target types come from explicitly
declared file-local fields and non-primary superclass constructors, including
forwarded super parameters. Primary-constructor fields and extension-type
representation fields are not visited. Missing or untyped targets are skipped.
Superclass lookup uses only the final name segment, so a prefixed superclass
can be confused with a local declaration. Likewise, identically spelled type
parameters from different scopes can compare equal without representing the
same type. A reported annotation is therefore not always safe to remove.

annotated `@awaitNotRequired` in this file are exempt; nullable or
unresolved types stay silent.

statement is `break;` is left alone: without it the case would be empty and
share the next case's body.

```dart

    log();
    break; // flagged
  case 2:
    break; // ok: keeps the case from sharing the next body
  default:

}
```

version predates Dart 3.0, where those `break`s prevent fall-through.

keyword on parameters, local variable statements, for-each loop variables
of `for` statements (including destructuring loops), pattern variable

Flags a redundant `late` modifier on an initialized static or top-level variable.

Static fields and top-level variables in Dart are already initialized lazily:
their initializer does not run until the variable is first read. Marking such
a declaration `late` therefore buys nothing, and it misleads readers into
thinking deferred initialization is significant here. The rule only fires when
the declarator actually has an initializer, since `late` on an uninitialized
static or top-level variable does carry meaning. Drop the `late` keyword.

Flags a null-aware access whose member comes from an extension on a nullable type.

An extension declared `on String?` already accepts `null`, so `s?.member`
skips a call the extension could handle, and `s.member` is what the author
means. The rule fires on `?.` property and method access and on `?[]`
index access when the target is an extension override (`E(s)?.member`) of
an extension on a nullable type, or when the target's static type is
nullable and every visible extension supplying that member to the type is
on a nullable type. Members the target's own class declares win over
extensions and are not checked; for SDK classes falcon uses the loaded SDK
sources, or without them its curated `dart:core` table (e.g.
`String.length`, `String.[]`).

Every section of a null-aware cascade (`x?..m()..n()`) is null-aware too;
each section's leading member is checked against the cascade target. An
extension on `dynamic` (or `void`) is on a nullable type.

Imported extensions participate even through prefixed imports, subject to
show/hide combinators and exports. Explicit overrides resolve the extension
by declaration identity, including qualified names. The rule stays silent
when it cannot tell which extensions apply.

docs:
Flags a null assertion `!` on a value that flows into a nullable context.

When `x!` is passed to a `String?` parameter, assigned to an `int?`
variable, or returned from a function returning `Object?`, the context
accepts `null` anyway: the `!` only adds a runtime failure. The rule
fires on `!` whose value directly is:

- the initializer of a variable or field declared with a nullable type;
- the right side of a plain `=` assignment to a nullable target other than
  a local variable or parameter (the `!` may promote those), unless the
  asserted operand is the assigned name itself (`x = x!`);
- an argument for a nullable parameter, except `Future.value(x!)` and
  `completer.complete(x!)`;
- returned from a top-level or local function (including async functions
  and top-level getters), or yielded to a nullable stream/iterable element,
  including `yield*` (matching the analyzer's element-type check);
- an element of a list or set literal, or a key or value of a map
  literal, whose element types are nullable;

and on a null-assert pattern `p!` of a pattern assignment whose matched
value is nullable. In declarations, `for` loops, and `case` clauses the
`!` narrows the bound variables, so it is never flagged there.

`dynamic` and `void` accept null too. Unresolved contexts stay silent.
Index writes and right-hand operator operands use their instantiated
parameter types, not the enclosing expression's result context.
Grouping parentheses preserve the nullable context of the inner assertion.

provably non-null value.

deliberately conservative about "provably non-null" — only literals (numbers,
strings, booleans, collections, records), constructor invocations, and function
expressions qualify; anything whose value flows from another binding is left
alone. It applies to final/const top-level variables, static fields, and local
variables. Drop the `?` from the declared type.

docs:
Flags parentheses that can be removed without changing the meaning or
hurting readability.

Parentheses are always reported when they sit directly inside other
parentheses, a string interpolation, the only argument of an argument list,
or the condition of an `if`, `while`, `do`, or `switch`. Elsewhere they are
reported around a single token (identifier, literal) or a null-aware chain
unless they are needed: before `.hashCode`/`.runtimeType`/`.toString()`/
`.noSuchMethod()`, before `!`, before a member of a nullable-type extension,
or around a null-aware index in a conditional `then` branch or map key.

Parentheses are kept around conditional expressions, type literals,
cascades and anything inside a cascade, function expressions in a constructor
field initializer, `==`/`!=` comparisons that are assigned, returned, or
yielded, a `switch` expression starting a statement, and expressions with
internal whitespace (binary, `as`, `is`, `await`, assignments, ...) unless
the parentheses are the whole right-hand side, return value, argument, or
record field. Inside another expression they are kept when the parent is a
binary, conditional, `as`, `is`, or function invocation, before a member
access on a prefix/postfix expression, and where removing them would turn a
set or map literal into a statement block.

Generic constructor tear-offs need parentheses when type arguments are
followed by invocation arguments (`(C.named)<T>()`), but not when the
instantiated tear-off is used as a value (`(C.named)<T>`). When constructor
signatures are unavailable, a type-qualified target is kept unless it is
known to be a nonconstructor member.

Explicit expression grouping is retained by the parser, including parentheses
separated from their expression by comments. Pattern grouping is not an
expression and is not reported. The official exemption for a parenthesized
non-record argument to a record-typed parameter (a missing trailing comma)
only applies to code that does not compile and is not modeled here.

```dart
a = (b);          // flagged
print((x));       // flagged
a = (b == c);     // ok
(b ? c : d).foo(); // ok
```
name: unnecessary-parenthesis

docs:
Report public declarations that no entry point of an executable library
reaches.

A library — its defining unit plus every `part` file — is executable when it
declares a top-level function named `main`, or a top-level function
annotated `@pragma('vm:entry-point')` whose `pragma` provably resolves to
`dart:core`. Starting from those entry points (and from top-level functions
annotated with a widget-preview `@Preview`), the rule follows references:
identifiers, invocations, constructor names and tear-offs, annotations,
user-defined operators, object-pattern fields, doc comment references,
supertypes named in a class's `extends`/`with`/`implements` clause or an
extension type's `implements` clause, implicit super-constructor calls,
typedef and extension-type names, type literals, type arguments, and the
types of `external` members. Type parameters shadow same-named library
declarations. A plain type annotation is not a reference, and
constructor invocations inside constant patterns do not count. Instance
`toJson` methods are reachable with their container, because `dart:convert`
calls them dynamically.

The candidates are the library's top-level declarations and the public
constructors (except enum constructors), fields, methods, getters, setters,
and operators of public classes, enums, mixins, extensions, and extension
types. A member that overrides a supertype member is not a candidate, nor
are the test-harness methods `test_*`, `solo_test_*`, `setUp`, `tearDown`,
`setUpClass`, and `tearDownClass`. Unreached public candidates are reported
unless annotated `@visibleForTesting` or a widget preview; a member other
than a field is not reported again when its enclosing declaration already
is (the analyzer reports unreachable fields of an unreachable class too).
Libraries that declare a top-level name twice are not analyzed.

Facts falcon cannot prove are resolved toward reachability, so uncertainty
causes misses rather than false positives: a member whose container has a
supertype with an incomplete indexed hierarchy may override it and is not
a candidate. Known receiver types resolve members and operators before
considering extensions. An unknown receiver reaches same-named members
only in extensions or classes named outside their own declaration (a class
never named cannot be its static type); an identifier counts unless it
resolves to a local. A library with a part that does not resolve to an
analyzed file is not analyzed.
name: unreachable-from-main

docs:
Flags construction of a widget or type that should be replaced by its design-system equivalent.

Teams building on a Flutter design system often want to steer away from raw
framework widgets (a bare `Container`, `Text`, or `ElevatedButton`) toward
their own wrappers, which enforce spacing, theming, and accessibility. This
rule flags a construction whose class name matches a configured entry, in
either constructor form — implicit `Foo(...)`, explicit `new`/`const`, and
generic `Foo<T>(...)`. It deliberately ignores named-constructor access like
`Foo.named(...)` so static getters and factory helpers are not mistaken for
plain construction. The rule is entirely config-driven: with no configured
items it is a no-op, so it flags nothing until a design system is described.

## Options

`items` (list of objects, default: `[]`) — each entry maps a `class_name`
(required) to steer away from, with an optional `use_instead` naming the
design-system replacement to suggest in the message.

Checks constructions throughout the program, including initializers and annotations.
name: use-design-system-item

docs:
Flags an old-style function-typed parameter written with inline parameter syntax.

Dart lets you declare a function-typed parameter two ways. The legacy form
inlines the callee's own parameter list — `void f(int g(int x))` — while the
modern generic function type syntax writes the type up front:
`void f(int Function(int) g)`. The modern form is preferred because it reads
as an ordinary typed parameter, composes with nullability (`Function(int)?`),
and keeps the parameter name in its usual place. The rule detects the old form
by the nested parameter list the parser attaches to it; the modern form parses
as a plain parameter with a function type and is not flagged. Rewrite using
`Function` type syntax. Diagnostics cover the complete parameter declaration.

runtime. Candidates are private (underscore) top-level variables and private

`abstract` declarations. Any other use — a plain read, a `this._x`
initializing formal, a `: _x = ...` initializer, a compound or `??=`
assignment, or an assignment whose value is not proven non-nullable —
disqualifies the referenced declaration. Qualified and cascade accesses are
attributed to their resolved declaration, not every implementation of an
interface member. Uses in every resolved library part are checked together;
unresolved parts prevent proving a candidate safe.

```dart
}
```

description: Prefers `throwsA` matchers over `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (...) {}`.
docs:
Prefers `throwsA` matchers over `try { ...; fail(...); } catch (...) {}`.

A `try` statement with a single `catch` clause, no `finally`, and a body
that ends in a call to the test framework's `fail` hand-rolls what
`expect(() => ..., throwsA(...))` states directly, and with worse failure
messages. Like the official rule, only the top-level `fail` declared in
`package:test_api/src/frontend/expect.dart` counts. Current `test_api`
releases no longer declare it there (`package:test`, `test_api`, and
`flutter_test` re-export `package:matcher`'s `fail`), so only code using
such an old `test_api` is reported; a local or member function named
`fail` never is. The declaring library is identified through the package
configuration, including when `test_api` is a dependency.

```dart
try {
  parse('');
  fail('Expected a FormatException');  // BAD
} on FormatException {}

expect(() => parse(''), throwsA(isA<FormatException>())); // GOOD
```
name: use-test-throws-matchers

docs:
Flags empty `catch` blocks.

A catch clause with no body silently swallows the exception, hiding failures
that should be handled, logged, or rethrown and making bugs far harder to
diagnose. Handle the error, or at minimum log it, rather than discarding it.
Two escape hatches match the official lint: a catch whose body contains a
comment (the emptiness is deliberate and documented), and a catch that binds
its exception to `_`, an explicit "I am ignoring this" marker.

This includes catch clauses inside anonymous functions.
name: empty-catches

docs:
Flags stray empty statements (a lone `;`).

A solitary semicolon does nothing, and where it slips in it usually changes
meaning: `while (cond);` turns the following block into an unconditional body,
and a stray `;` after an `if` header detaches the intended branch. It is
almost always an accidental extra semicolon or a loop body that should have
been a block. Remove it, or replace it with the block that was intended. The
semicolons in a `for (;;)` header are loop syntax, not statements, and are
never reported. A real `null;` expression statement is not an empty statement.

This includes empty statements inside anonymous functions.
name: empty-statements

An empty function, method, loop, or switch-case body is frequently an

docs:
Flags an argument passed more than once in the same invocation.

When two arguments to a call or constructor have identical source text — such
as `Point(x, x)` where one was meant to be `y` — the repetition is usually a
copy-paste slip that silently produces wrong results. Positional arguments are
compared against other positional arguments by source text, and named
arguments against other named arguments by their value expression (the label
is ignored); a positional is never matched against a named. Literal-valued
arguments are excluded, since repeating a literal like `Size(48, 48)` is
intentional. The report lands on the last duplicate.
name: no-equal-arguments

docs:
Flags an `if`/`else` or ternary whose two branches are identical.

When the then and else branches have the same body, the condition decides
nothing — the same code runs either way — so either the condition is pointless
or one branch was never edited to differ. Comparison is on branch source text
with whitespace outside strings and comments normalized away, so formatting
differences do not hide a match while literal and comment contents stay intact. Remove the condition and keep the single body, or correct
the branch that was supposed to differ. Applies to both `if`/`else` statements
and `?:` ternary expressions.
name: no-equal-then-else

Flags proven self-comparisons of side-effect-free scalar values.

Getter reads, index operations, calls, and user-defined operator receivers are
intentionally excluded: evaluating the same syntax twice need not produce the
same value, and equality/ordering may be overloaded.
A scalar read type does not establish stability: unqualified top-level and
inherited getter names still execute a getter on each evaluation.

docs:
Flags references to a wildcard variable or parameter (a name made solely of
underscores, such as `_` or `__`).

An all-underscore name marks a binding as intentionally unused, and under
Dart's wildcard-variable semantics such names are non-binding — reading one
back does not retrieve the value you expect. Referencing it is therefore
either a mistake or a reliance on behavior that is changing. Declaring a
wildcard is fine; only uses in expression position are reported. Give the
binding a real name if you actually need its value.
name: no-wildcard-variable-uses

docs:
Flags instance fields that redeclare an inherited field.

A field is reported when its inherited concrete super implementation is a
field — the first concrete getter-providing member of the superclass chain
and mixin applications, or for a mixin the member of its `on` types'
interfaces (`Object` without one). Fields reached only through `implements`,
abstract members of superclasses, and fields shadowed by a nearer getter or
method are not reported; covariance does not matter. Extension types
inherit no concrete members.
Declaring `var`/`final` primary constructor parameters are instance fields
too; forwarding formals and ordinary header parameters are not declarations.
name: overridden-fields

docs:
Flags a getter that unconditionally returns itself.

A body of `=> x` (or `=> this.x`, or `return x;`) inside `get x` calls the
getter again with no base case, recursing until the stack overflows at
runtime. It almost always means a backing field was intended — typically an
underscore-prefixed `_x` — but was misspelled as the getter's own name.
Return the backing field instead. Only a direct, unconditional self-reference
is reported; a getter that merely mentions its own name inside a larger
expression is left alone.
name: recursive-getters

docs:
Flags `x ??= null`, which can never have an effect.

The `??=` operator assigns only when the target is currently null, so
assigning `null` is a guaranteed no-op: a null target stays null, and
otherwise nothing happens. Such a statement is dead code that usually points
to a mistaken right-hand side — the author likely meant a real default value.
Remove the statement, or supply the value that was intended.
name: unnecessary-null-aware-assignments

docs:
Flags `x ?? null` and `null ?? x`, where the `null` operand is redundant.

The `??` operator falls back to its right operand only when the left is null,
so `x ?? null` always evaluates to `x` and `null ?? x` always evaluates to
`x`. The literal `null` contributes nothing and typically marks an unfinished
edit or a misunderstanding of the operator. Delete the `null` operand, and the
`??` along with it.
name: unnecessary-null-in-if-null-operators

docs:
Flags `throw e` inside a `catch (e)` by matching the exception parameter's name.

Re-throwing the caught object with `throw e` starts a fresh stack trace from
the catch site, discarding the original point of failure and making the error
far harder to trace. Use `rethrow`, which propagates the same exception with
its trace intact. Matching is syntactic: the thrown identifier must have the
exception parameter's spelling; binding identity is not resolved. Throws
inside a nested closure or a nested `try`/`catch` are skipped.
name: use-rethrow-when-possible
